Hm, what exactly do you mean by "more accessible"?
Well, the implementation doesn't need to worry about enforcing locking, just providing something like a mutex implementation in the interface if they feel locking is an issue
If they don't need locking that can be a no-op - it leaves the choice up to the OS developer rather than enforcing a CDI design choice on them
It does however mean driver writers need to write code which locks global structures when they're used and all that
Hm, what you describe is basically threading, no?
For one definition of threading
It might be coming from a completely different process context, but I guess it's still a thread
The async model would mean that you don't need locks because threading is forbidden, but each function like send_packet gets a callback as an additional parameter
At least that's how I understand it
Well, I think it should be possible for multiple contexts to call upon a driver
The context usually doesn't make a difference in kernel space, does it?
In Pedigree for example you can have many threads all calling into the same device driver
(system calls are pre-emptable by the scheduler)
Well, yes
You're confusing me
Are we actually talking about the same thing, just with different names?
Possibly
Because this is exactly my definition of the threading solution, whereas you said "remove threads"
Well, the CDI implementation doesn't create threads, which is how you defined it earlier
The Pedigree kernel is the CDI implementation
"run multiple threads" interpreted as "create multiple threads"
No, the CDI implementation is the CDI module which sits between the kernel and CDI drivers
The interface != the kernel
It implements the interface by means of the kernel, so the kernel is part of the implementation ;-)
Okay, I'll s/CDI implementation/OS/ then. Better this way?
Well in that case my mention of "remove threads" is the opposite of what I want ;)
Right, so I guess we actually mean the same

pcmattman: Are you okay with making this kind of threading opt-in? Like adding a field cdi_driver.threadsafe and if it's not set, the CDI implementation must lock the device before calling into the driver if the OS uses threads?

CDI implementation rather

So the question is: is the threading opt-in to be an opt-in provided by the CDI implementation (eg, turning cdi_mutex_lock into a no-op)?
(that would mean drivers would need to be fully aware of potential locking, but the OS developer could ignore the lock requests if they wanted)
Or should it be on the other side?
What I was thinking about is that driver can completely ignore the whole issue and get a global lock from the CDI implementation if needed.
Their performance will probably suffer, but a simple working driver is better than no driver at all
What the CDI implementation actually is doing with lock requests, is up to the OS anyway. If the OS uses threads, it should probably do locking. If not, make it a no-op.
